extracted.intended_audience: Wikipedia readers and editors; people researching notable incidents of scientific misconduct
extracted.subtask_description: A dynamic Wikipedia list documenting notable incidents of scientific misconduct across disciplines, with brief descriptions of cases, types of wrongdoing, and (explicit) inclusion guidance for what incidents belong on the page.

rubrics_metrics.name: Inclusion criterion for the list
rubrics_metrics.description: Incidents should only be included in this list if the individuals or entities involved have their own Wikipedia articles, or in the absence of an article, where the misconduct incident is covered in multiple reliable sources.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The page is a dynamic list; editors are asked to add missing items only with references to reliable sources. Notability (having a Wikipedia article) is a primary filter; otherwise multiple reliable-source coverage of the incident is required.

rubrics_metrics.name: General definition of scientific misconduct
rubrics_metrics.description: Scientific misconduct is a serious form of violation of the standard codes of scholarly conduct and ethical behavior in the publication of professional scientific research.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The article frames incidents as violations of scholarly/ethical standards in research publication; entries are case examples of such violations and their consequences (retractions, investigations, bans, criminal charges).

rubrics_metrics.name: Denmark definition (example from Lancet review)
rubrics_metrics.description: In Denmark, scientific misconduct is defined as "intention[al] negligence leading to fabrication of the scientific message or a false credit or emphasis given to a scientist".
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This phrasing is quoted as an example of a policy definition of misconduct; it emphasizes intentional negligence, fabrication of the scientific message, and wrongful attribution or credit.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sweden definition (example from Lancet review)
rubrics_metrics.description: In Sweden [misconduct is defined] as "intention[al] distortion of the research process by fabrication of data, text, hypothesis, or methods from another researcher's manuscript form or publication; or distortion of the research process in other ways."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This policy-style definition highlights fabrication of data/text/hypotheses/methods and broader distortions of the research process as constitutive of misconduct.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fabrication and falsification of data
rubrics_metrics.description: Making up data or altering/forging results and experimental records (examples in the article include fabricated clinical trials, invented data sets, adding antibodies to samples to alter results, and forged experimental records).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The page gives many concrete examples (e.g., Darsee, Fujii, Dipak Das, Dong-Pyou Han) and documents typical consequences: retractions, loss of funding, institutional sanctions, prison sentences, and reputation damage. Fabrication/falsification is treated as core misconduct.

rubrics_metrics.name: Plagiarism (including proposal/grant and publication plagiarism)
rubrics_metrics.description: Copying text, ideas, or whole works without attribution, including plagiarism of grant applications, proposals, or books (examples include plagiarized NIH/NSF proposals and journal articles).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples (e.g., Leo Paquette, Vishwa Jit Gupta, multiple philosophy and humanities cases) show penalties ranging from retractions and degree revocation to institutional sanctions. The article treats plagiarism as a common and well-documented form of misconduct.

rubrics_metrics.name: Image manipulation and figure falsification
rubrics_metrics.description: Manipulating images or figures in published papers (duplication, inappropriate re-use or digital alteration of images) to misrepresent results.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Several cases are cited (e.g., Silvia Bulfone-Paus, Olivier Voinnet, Lesné) where image manipulation led to retractions, expressions of concern, or corrections; the page uses such cases to illustrate this category.

rubrics_metrics.name: Authorship and contributor misconduct (forgery, fake co-authors, false credit)
rubrics_metrics.description: False or fraudulent authorship practices: inventing co-authors, forging signatures, misattributing credit, publishing without co-author consent, or using false names/emails to manipulate processes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples include forged co-authors (Fujii), publishing without a co-author's consent (Gideon Koren), and using false identities to peer-review one's own papers (Moon Hyung-in). Consequences include retractions, professional sanctions, and degree revocations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Peer-review fraud and compromised peer-review
rubrics_metrics.description: Manipulating or faking the peer-review process (fake reviews, compromised editorial/peer-review procedures, rings of fake reviewers).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The article references large-scale publisher retractions and investigations (e.g., fake peer reviews leading to mass retractions), and individual cases where compromised peer review led to retractions and loss of trust in published work.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ethics violations in human/animal research and lack of approval
rubrics_metrics.description: Conducting experiments without proper ethical approval or consent, coercing participants or staff, or otherwise violating human/animal-subjects protections (examples: He Jiankui's embryo editing, Macchiarini's false claims of ethical approval and coercion).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Such violations are treated as serious misconduct with legal and professional consequences (prison sentences, fines, institutional investigations, retractions, clinical trial suspensions).

rubrics_metrics.name: Grant fraud and financial/administrative misconduct
rubrics_metrics.description: Falsifying information on grant applications, misusing funds, embezzlement, or other financial misconduct connected to research (examples: Eric Poehlman's grant fraud; Penkowa's embezzlement).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consequences documented include criminal convictions, funding bans, salary/position loss, and retractions of associated publications.

rubrics_metrics.name: Data-source fraud and implausible/ fabricated datasets
rubrics_metrics.description: Reporting or publishing studies based on fabricated or implausible underlying data sources (e.g., companies or data providers that claimed non-existent hospital records), leading to paper retractions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Surgisphere example is cited where high-profile articles were retracted after data were found implausible; the page treats implausible/opaque data provenance as grounds for serious concern and retraction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Self-plagiarism and duplicate/ redundant publication
rubrics_metrics.description: Reusing one's own previously published text or data without proper disclosure or publishing overlapping/duplicate articles (self-plagiarism, concurrent publications).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples (e.g., Bruno Frey, others) show journals issuing retractions or corrections; the article treats self-plagiarism as a notable breach of publication ethics.

rubrics_metrics.name: Statistical and methodological manipulation (post-hoc changes, omitted data)
rubrics_metrics.description: Altering research design after the fact, adding control groups post hoc, omitting data, or using problematic statistical techniques to misrepresent findings.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The page cites cases (e.g., Lorenza Colzato, LaCour, others) where methodological irregularities and falsified analyses led to retractions and rescinded appointments; such manipulations are flagged as misconduct rather than honest error when intentional or systemic.
